cim: Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Neurosurgery: Balancing Innovation with Responsibility
cim_eredeti: Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Neurosurgery: Balancing Innovation with Responsibility
szoveg_eredeti:
October 27, 2026 - Featured in the CNS Quarterly

Artificial intelligence (AI) is entering neurosurgery not as a single disruptive event, but as a series of increasingly routine tools.

It is appearing in documentation platforms, inbox management, radiographic analysis, scheduling, patient communication, and early decision-support systems. In many institutions, AI is already participating in care in some form, and it is moving quickly while the policies governing its use are still developing.

For neurosurgeons, the central question is no longer whether AI will influence clinical practice. A recent systematic review highlights expanding applications across diagnosis, prognosis, surgical planning, and intraoperative workflows, alongside persistent concerns around bias, interpretability, validation, and ethics. The more important question is how these tools can be implemented in a manner that preserves patient trust, professional accountability, and the ethical standards of the specialty.

If AI struggles to achieve durable adoption in medicine, it may not be because the models lack capability, but because patients, physicians, health systems, regulators, and vendors fail to establish clear expectations for its use. Here we outline the ethical and legal considerations surrounding the implementation of AI in neurosurgery, aiming to reinforce best practices while promoting adoption when beneficial.

The first ethical challenge is also the most immediate: AI systems depend on data.

Neurosurgical patients entrust physicians with some of the most sensitive information in medicine, including imaging studies, neurological diagnoses, genetic information, cognitive assessments, operative videos, and longitudinal medical histories. These data may be valuable for building better tools, but they remain deeply personal and require careful stewardship.

Ambient documentation platforms illustrate this tension clearly. These tools may reduce documentation burden and allow physicians to spend more time facing patients rather than screens. That is a meaningful improvement. However, when clinical conversations are recorded and transmitted to third-party servers to be processed by AI systems, questions of consent, disclosure, and data handling become immediate.

Recent litigation involving health systems using AI note-taking tools has alleged that patient-provider conversations were recorded and processed without adequate consent. Regardless of the legal outcomes, these cases highlight the importance of implementation details. Patients may be comfortable with AI-assisted documentation, particularly if it improves the clinical interaction, but far less so if they later learn that their visit was recorded, transmitted, or processed in ways they did not understand.

AI should not be treated as an invisible layer of clinical infrastructure. Patients do not need a technical explanation of every algorithm used within a health system, but they deserve meaningful transparency when AI is listening, summarizing, recommending, or otherwise influencing their care. The legal framework may center on consent, but the underlying ethical issue is trust.

AI systems increasingly generate outputs that appear polished, structured, and authoritative. That presentation is part of their value, but it can also obscure uncertainty: a well-formatted note, a confident risk estimate, or a clear recommendation may create an impression of reliability—even when the underlying model is wrong, incomplete, or poorly calibrated.

Current legal scholarship continues to place responsibility for medical decision-making on the treating physician. AI may assist with documentation, pattern recognition, triage, risk prediction, or decision support, but ultimate liability still falls on the human—an appropriate standard.

As a result, automation bias remains a real concern. As AI tools become embedded in clinical workflows, disagreeing with the model may begin to feel like an exception that requires justification—useful when the model is accurate and appropriately applied, but dangerous when it is poorly validated, used outside its intended context, or insensitive to patient-specific factors.

The standard of care remains human. AI may augment clinical judgment, but it does not replace professional responsibility or liability. For the foreseeable future, physicians will remain responsible for understanding when to use AI, when to question it, and when to ignore it.

Much of the excitement surrounding AI focuses on model performance: accuracy, speed, scale, and new capabilities. In clinical practice, however, the model is only one component. Equally important are the processes surrounding it: how the tool is evaluated, deployed, monitored, updated, audited, and explained.

One encouraging development has been the emergence of practical implementation frameworks from groups such as the Coalition for Health AI, whose guidance emphasizes local validation, monitoring, appropriate policies, and governance structures adaptable to individual health systems. These efforts recognize that deployment is not the end of evaluation; in many respects, it is the beginning.

This distinction is particularly important for AI. Traditional medical devices are often evaluated as relatively static tools, whereas AI systems may behave differently across institutions, patient populations, and clinical environments. A model that performs well in one dataset may not generalize to another, bias may not become apparent until after deployment, and performance can drift over time.

For neurosurgery, these issues are especially relevant: our datasets are often smaller, pathologies heterogeneous, and decisions highly context-dependent. A model trained broadly may not generalize cleanly to a pediatric epilepsy conference, a spine deformity clinic, a skull base tumor board, or a ruptured aneurysm in the middle of the night.

Responsible adoption therefore requires more than procurement; it requires institutional ownership. Health systems need clear policies on which tools may be used, what data may be shared, how vendors are evaluated, how performance is monitored, and how clinicians can report concerns. Governance should include clinicians, data scientists, administrators, legal experts, ethicists, and, when possible, patient representatives.

The legal and ethical concerns surrounding AI are substantial, but they should not obscure the potential benefits.

If the more optimistic projections prove correct, AI could make clinical life better: practices may run more smoothly, documentation may become less burdensome, and the electronic medical record may evolve from a system that demands information into one that organizes it—physicians spending less time as data-entry clerks and more time caring for patients.

Care delivery may also become more precise. AI systems may help identify patients at higher risk for complications, personalize perioperative pathways, and support earlier intervention when patients begin to deteriorate. In the operating room, computer vision and multimodal systems may eventually improve visualization, navigation, operative documentation, and training. Surgical education may become more objective, with automated feedback from operative video complementing traditional apprenticeship, and brain-computer interfaces may change how humans interact with computers writ large.

AI may also serve a quieter but equally important function: ensuring that vulnerable patients are not lost to follow-up. The high-risk patients most likely to slip through the cracks of a fragmented system are often those with the fewest resources to advocate for themselves. Tools that flag these patients, prompt outreach, and surface those who would otherwise be overlooked can act as a form of advocacy.
